attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, stated in his own voice and not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: The normalisation matches the statement: a firm present-tense claim that LLMs fall well short of near-100% clarity on user intentions. The threshold wording is kept and nothing is added.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: it limits the claim to models of the time and asks for recurring, material misinterpretation, short of near-perfect. It also separates misunderstanding from execution and feasibility failures. The period ending at the post date is reasonable.

evidence.note: The SayCan paper (2022-08-16, within the period) says vanilla SayCan does not handle negation, a limitation inherited from the underlying LLMs. That is a language-interpretation failure. Chain-of-thought prompting improved it but does not show near-perfect reliability.

Peer-reviewed workshop paper, May 2022: GPT-3 performed mostly at chance on tests of implied meaning and presupposition. It is an indirect probe, but it supports material shortfalls in grasping intended meaning.

Company disclosure: 84% planning success and examples where requests were interpreted correctly. This shows partial success but not near-perfect interpretation, and the planning rate mixes in non-language factors. It qualifies the claim but does not contradict it.

reviews.rationale: Supported. Two 2022 evaluations show recurring language-interpretation failures: SayCan's negation limitation inherited from the LLM (e1), and GPT-3 near chance on implied meaning (e2). The best counterevidence, e3, reports 84% planning success, which is well short of near-perfect. Nothing in the packet meets the contradiction condition of broad, near-perfect interpretation.
